cases.message: Why did my score drop from 611 to 588 this month?

routing.reason: The member asks why their score dropped 23 points, which is a score-change question; a higher reported card balance is a common cause of a drop, so utilization is also relevant.

cases.reply:
Your score moved from 611 on 2026-09-15 to 588 now (VantageScore 3.0). Two things in your profile likely explain it, biggest first.

**1. The late payment.** Your retail store card was reported 30 days late on 2026-09-28, for the payment due 2026-08-25. A new late payment of 30 days or more usually weighs more than anything else on a report. You paid the past-due amount on 2026-10-02 and the account is current again, which is the right move. The late mark itself can stay on your report for its full reporting period, though.

**2. Higher utilization.** Utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) rose. Your balances were reported at $1,410 of $3,000 in limits, which is 47%, up from $900 (30%) the month before. Under 30% is the common guidance, and under 10% tends to be better.

Per card:
- Retail store card: $900 of $1,500 (60%)
- Bank credit card: $510 of $1,500 (34%)

Other things look neutral here. You have one hard inquiry in the last 12 months, from April, and nothing new this month. Your Credit Builder payments are all on time.

Utilization is the part you can change fastest. Under most current models, a high-balance effect eases once a lower balance is reported, usually after the next statement. I can't predict how many points that would change or when your score would hit a certain level.

Next step: Pay down the retail store card before its statement closing date so a lower balance gets reported.

cases.message: I've never missed a payment, so why did my score go down 13 points?

routing.reason: The member asks why their score dropped 13 points despite never missing a payment, which is a score-changes question; a higher reported utilization is a common cause of a drop, so utilization also applies.

cases.reply:
Your score went from 668 on 2026-09-15 to 655 now (VantageScore 3.0). Your payment history is clean, so a late payment isn't the cause. The most likely reason is higher card balances.

**What changed**
- On 2026-09-20, a car repair was charged to your Rewards credit card.
- On 2026-10-05, your balances were reported at $2,550 against $3,000 in limits. That is 85% utilization (how much of your card limits you're using). It was $2,100, or 70%, the month before.
- Your Rewards card is at 95% of its limit ($1,900 of $2,000). Your Bank card is at 65% ($650 of $1,000). Scoring models look at each card as well as the overall total.

Common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better. Your Credit Builder plan is an installment loan, so it isn't part of this ratio. Your profile shows no new hard inquiries, no new accounts, and no negative items, so nothing else explains the move.

**Will it come back?**
I can't say how many points or when. Issuers usually report your statement balance once a month. Under most current scoring models, high utilization stops weighing on the score once a lower balance is reported, usually after the next statement. The rest of your credit report still matters too.

**What may help**
- Pay down the Rewards card before its statement closing date, so a lower balance gets reported.
- Make extra payments during the month instead of one payment.
- Keep your older no-fee cards open.

Your on-time payments are a real strength. This dip comes from reported balances, not from anything you did wrong.

Next step: Check your Rewards card's statement closing date, and make a payment before that date so a lower balance gets reported.

cases.message: A lender told me I don't have a FICO score. How long until I get one?

routing.reason: The member has little or no credit history and asks how long until they get a FICO score, which matches the credit-builder-account skill's scope for people with little or no credit history asking how to start building and how long until they have a score.

cases.reply:
That's a common spot for someone new to credit, Maya, and it's fixable with time.

A FICO score needs two things: at least one account open for 6 months or more, and at least one account reported in the past 6 months. Your profile shows your Credit Builder plan opened on 2026-06-01, so it has been open about 4.5 months. It is reported monthly, which covers the second requirement.

So the plan is on track to meet both. I can't give you an exact date or promise a score, since that depends on the scoring model and what's on your credit report. The lender's check on 2026-09-02 came before the 6-month mark, which fits with no FICO score then.

Meanwhile, you do have a VantageScore 3.0 of 612, up from 603 a month ago. Some lenders use FICO and some use VantageScore, so you may see different results depending on who checks.

What helps most right now is simple: keep paying on time. You've made 4 on-time payments and have 20 left. Your next payment is due 2026-11-01.

Next step: Pay your Credit Builder payment on or before 2026-11-01.

cases.message: When will the phone company collection come off my credit report?

routing.reason: The member asks when a phone company collection will fall off their report, which is squarely a collections question about how long collection accounts stay.

cases.reply:
Your profile shows the phone company collection has an original delinquency date (the date you first fell behind) of March 14, 2022. A collection can stay on your reports for up to 7 years from that date, so it would be expected to drop off around March 2029.

A few things to know:

- **Paying or resale doesn't restart the clock.** If you pay it, or the debt is sold to another collector, the 7-year period still counts from March 2022.
- **Paying doesn't remove it.** A paid collection shows as paid. Your profile shows this one as unpaid at $1,200.
- **Scoring models differ.** Your score is VantageScore 3.0, which ignores paid collections. Some other models, like FICO 8, can still count them. I can't promise a specific score change either way.

Because this debt is older, be careful before you make any payment or sign anything promising to pay. In many states, that can restart the deadline for being sued over the debt. I can't tell you whether your debt is past that deadline. A legal aid office or an attorney can check your state's rules. This is general information, not legal advice.

Your profile also shows a letter from the collection agency on September 22. If you don't recognize the debt or think the amount is wrong, the letter may list a validation period (30 days after you received it) in which you can dispute in writing. That window may be close to ending or already over, so check the date on the letter.

Next step: Check the validation period end date on the September 22 letter, and if you have any doubt about the debt, contact a legal aid office or attorney before you pay or promise anything.

cases.message: If I pay my next Credit Builder payment a few days late, will it hurt my score?

routing.reason: The member asks whether a few-days-late Credit Builder payment hurts, which is covered by credit-builder-account; a late payment's effect on the report also touches payment-history.

cases.reply:
A few days late should not be reported as late. Credit Builder payments are reported as late only once they are 30 or more days past due. A payment 1 to 29 days late is not reported as late.

Your profile shows your next payment is due 2026-11-01. You have made 7 on time and have 0 late payments, so your record on this plan is clean.

A few things to keep in mind:

- **Fees and other effects:** I don't have details on what happens if you pay late, such as fees, so I can't say. Human support can confirm.
- **Don't let it slip past day 30.** A late mark is reported in steps (30, 60, 90 days and beyond), and it can stay on your reports for up to 7 years. Late payments are the biggest piece of a score, since payment history is about 35% of a FICO score.
- **Your cards matter too.** Your credit card balances are $2,550 against $3,000 in limits (85%). Paying those down is a separate way to help your score, and I can't predict how much your score would change.

If cash is tight around the due date, setting a reminder or autopay for the $6 can help you avoid the issue entirely.

Next step: Set a reminder for a few days before 2026-11-01 so the Credit Builder payment goes out on time.

cases.message: Should I apply for one of the credit cards I saw in the Marketplace?

routing.reason: The member asks whether to apply for a credit card seen in the Marketplace, which is covered by marketplace-offers (whether a new card fits their situation, approval odds, hard inquiry).

cases.reply:
Applying can be reasonable for you, and it's your call. Marketplace partners may pay the app when a user is approved. The app doesn't know your approval odds, and the issuer makes the decision.

**What your profile shows**
- Your only account is the Credit Builder plan, opened 4 months ago. It's current, with 4 on-time payments and no late ones.
- You have no negative items and no hard inquiries (checks that lenders run when you apply) in the last 12 months.
- Your VantageScore 3.0 is 612, up from 603 a month ago.
- You have no credit card, so you have no utilization (how much of your card limits you use) yet.

**The tradeoff**
- A card could add a second type of account and a credit limit. If you use it lightly and pay on time, that can help over time.
- Applying through a partner usually triggers a hard inquiry, which can affect your score. A new account also lowers the average age of your accounts, which matters more when your file is thin.
- Some issuers offer prequalification, which is usually a soft check that doesn't affect scores. It isn't approval. Check the offer page to see if it's available.

**Before you apply**
Compare the APR (yearly interest rate), fees, and terms on each offer page. Offer terms aren't in my data.

Also, a lender's check on 2026-09-02 found no FICO score for you. Some lenders may use FICO, so that could matter for approval. I can't say how any issuer will decide.

Next step: Look for a prequalification option on the offer you liked, so you can see what you may qualify for before a hard inquiry.

cases.message: How much will the Debt Settlement service cost me for my $2,800 card?

routing.reason: The member asks what the Debt Settlement service costs for a $2,800 card, which is covered by the debt-settlement skill's fee of 20% of the amount saved and when it is charged.

cases.reply:
**Short answer:** Nothing so far, and the fee depends on what the creditor agrees to. Your profile shows $0 in fees charged. The Bank credit card ($2,800) is still in negotiation, with no settlement agreed as of October 8.

**How the fee works:** It is 20% of the amount saved (the balance minus the settlement amount). It is charged only after a settlement is agreed and you make at least one payment under it. There are no upfront fees.

**Example only, not a prediction:** If $2,800 were settled for $2,000:
- Amount saved: $800
- Fee: $160
- Total you'd pay: $2,160

I can't say what the creditor will accept, and they don't have to agree to anything.

**Two other costs to know about:**
- **Taxes:** Forgiven debt may count as taxable income, even if no Form 1099-C arrives. A 1099-C usually comes when $600 or more is forgiven. Some exclusions exist, such as insolvency (IRS Publication 4681). This isn't tax advice, so a tax professional can tell you how it applies to you.
- **Credit report:** A settled account is usually reported as "settled for less than the full balance." It stays on your report, and a settled charge-off still shows as a charge-off.

**Good to know before you pay:** Get the terms in writing first. Because this is an old debt, check the statute of limitations (the time limit for a lawsuit) before any payment or signed agreement. Negotiating doesn't stop the creditor from collecting or suing. An attorney or legal aid office can advise you on that.

You can also negotiate directly with the creditor for free, or work with a nonprofit credit counselor.

Next step: Ask the creditor for any settlement offer in writing, and review it with a tax professional before you pay.

cases.message: My phone, electric and internet bills don't show up on my Experian report. Is Bill Reporting broken?

routing.reason: The member asks why utility, phone, and internet bills are missing from their Experian report, which is exactly what the bill-reporting skill covers since those payments are reported only to Equifax.

cases.reply:
No, this is expected. Bill Reporting sends your on-time payments to Equifax only. It does not send them to Experian or TransUnion, so they won't appear on your Experian report.

Your profile shows Bill Reporting is active, with 8 months reported for each of your three bills: mobile phone, electric utility, and home internet. Only on-time payments are reported. Late bills are never reported through the app.

Two other things may help:
- **Check Equifax.** Your bill history should be on your Equifax report, not Experian.
- **Rent is different.** The app reports rent to Experian and TransUnion, not Equifax.

Also, a score based only on Experian or TransUnion data won't reflect these bill payments. Your profile doesn't say which bureau your VantageScore 3.0 of 702 comes from, so I can't tell you whether bill data is part of it.

If the bills are missing from your Equifax report too, contact human support. They can check whether the payments are being detected in your linked bank account. You can reach them in the app at Help > Chat with support, or at support@example.com.

Next step: Look at your Equifax report and confirm the phone, electric and internet bills appear there.

cases.message: How long will the late payment from 2024 stay on my credit report?

routing.reason: The member asks how long a 2024 late payment stays on their report, which is a payment-history question about reporting duration and fade.

cases.reply:
The late payment on your bank credit card can stay on your reports for up to 7 years from the original delinquency date. Your profile shows that date as 2024-11-12, so it can remain until about November 2031. The mark was reported as 30 days late on 2024-12-16.

A few things to know:

- **Closing the account won't remove it sooner.** The late mark stays either way.
- **Its impact fades with time.** A late payment matters most while it is recent. As it ages and your on-time payments add up, it counts for less. Your card is open and current now, and your 4 months of on-time rent reporting add to your positive history.
- **Removal isn't something anyone can force.** If the late is accurate, it can legally stay for its full period. You can ask your card issuer for a goodwill removal (a letter asking them to remove it as a courtesy). It works best for a one-time slip on an otherwise clean account. They don't have to agree, so treat it as optional with no promised outcome.
- **Disputes are only for errors.** If any detail looks wrong, such as the date or the number of days late, you can dispute it with the bureau and the card issuer. You can check your reports for free at AnnualCreditReport.com.

Since you plan to apply for a mortgage in 2027, keeping every payment on time and setting autopay or reminders for at least the minimum on your card and auto loan will help most from here.

Next step: Pull your free reports at AnnualCreditReport.com and confirm the late payment's dates match what's shown here.

Your VantageScore 3.0 went from 611 on 2026-09-15 to 588 now. Two things in your profile likely explain it, biggest first:

- **The late payment.** Your retail store card was reported 30 days late on 2026-09-28. A new late payment usually weighs more than other changes. You paid the past-due amount on 2026-10-02, so the account is current. The late mark can still stay on your report.
- **Higher utilization (how much of your card limits you're using).** It is now 47% ($1,410 of $3,000), up from 30% the month before. Under 30% is the common guidance.

I can't say how many points either one cost you.

It shipped on 2026-10-06. The expected delivery window is 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-21, so it is not late yet. If it hasn't arrived by 2026-10-21, you can go to Card > Report not received. Once it arrives, activate it in the app before first use.

I'd wait. Your late payment was reported recently, and applying now risks a denial plus a hard inquiry (a lender check that can lower scores a little). Paying down balances costs nothing and needs no inquiry. If you do apply later, compare the APR, fees, and terms on the offer page. Marketplace partners may pay the app when a user is approved. I also can't tell you your approval odds.

Next step: Pay down your retail store card ($900 balance on a $1,500 limit) before its statement closing date, so a lower balance gets reported.

cases.message: When will my Credit Builder payments start showing on my credit report? And should I also get a secured card?

routing.reason: The member asks when Credit Builder payments are reported, which falls under credit-builder-account, and whether to also get a secured card, which falls under secured-card.

cases.reply:
**1. When payments show on your report**

They already do. Your profile shows you've made 4 on-time Credit Builder payments, and the plan started on June 1, 2026. Each payment is reported to Equifax, Experian and TransUnion as an installment account (a loan with fixed payments and an end date). Reporting happens monthly, a few days after the payment posts. Your most recent payment was October 1, so it may already be reported. Your VantageScore 3.0 is 612 now, up from 603 on September 15. I can't predict future changes.

Your next payment is due November 1. Paying on time keeps your record clean.

**2. Should you get a secured card?**

It could be reasonable, but it's your call. Right now you have no revolving account (like a credit card, where you borrow and repay each month). Your profile shows no card and no hard inquiries (credit checks) in the last 12 months. A card would add a second kind of account.

Here is what to weigh:
- You'd put down a refundable deposit of $50 to $2,000. That money is set aside, and your limit equals the deposit.
- Applying does not trigger a hard inquiry, and there's no annual fee.
- The APR (yearly interest rate) is a variable 27.99% on balances you carry from month to month.
- Late or missed payments get reported, and balances are reported monthly. Paying before the statement date lowers the reported balance.

cases.message: Will my reported rent help me get a mortgage in 2027? And does my auto loan count toward my utilization?

routing.reason: The member asks two things: whether reported rent will help a mortgage (rent-reporting) and whether an auto loan counts toward utilization (utilization, which covers whether a loan balance counts).

cases.reply:
**1. Will your reported rent help with a mortgage?**

It might, but it depends on the lender. I can't promise it will.

- Your profile shows 4 months of on-time rent reported ($1,400 a month). Rent Reporting sends this to TransUnion and Experian, not Equifax.
- Your score of 641 is a VantageScore 3.0, a model that can count rent. FICO 8 ignores rent.
- For mortgages sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, lenders can use Classic FICO (older versions that ignore rent) or VantageScore 4.0 (which can count rent). Since September 2026, any approved lender may choose VantageScore 4.0. Each lender decides.
- You chose not to add past rent. Your lease started 2024-09-01, and up to 12 months of past rent can be added for a one-time $25 fee. It's optional, and it would only add more positive history, not a set score change.

**2. Does your auto loan count toward utilization?**

No. Utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) only counts revolving accounts, like credit cards. An auto loan is an installment loan, with fixed payments, so it's left out.

Your profile shows overall utilization at 22%: $550 owed on a $2,500 limit. That's under the common 30% guideline. Under 10% tends to be better.

Your auto loan still matters in other ways, such as your payment history.

Next step: When you start talking to mortgage lenders, ask each one which score model and which credit bureaus it uses.

cases.message: Should I pay the $1,200 phone collection? And can your Debt Settlement service handle it?

routing.reason: The member asks whether to pay a $1,200 collection account, which falls under collections, and whether the Debt Settlement service can handle it, which falls under debt-settlement.

cases.reply:
**1. Should you pay the $1,200 phone collection?**

That is your call. Here are the trade-offs for this account.

- Paying does not remove it. It would show as paid. Your score model is VantageScore 3.0, which ignores paid collections, so paying may help. Other lenders use other models, and no one can promise a score change.
- The original missed payment was March 14, 2022. A collection can stay on your report up to 7 years from that date, so it would drop off around March 2029. Paying or a sale to another collector does not restart that clock.
- Before you pay or sign anything in writing, know that on old debts a partial payment or a written promise to pay can restart the legal deadline for being sued in many states. I can't say what your state's deadline is. A legal aid office or an attorney can check this for you. This is not legal advice.
- You got a letter from the collector on September 22. If the amount looks wrong or you don't recognize the debt, you can ask for validation and dispute it. If the debt is accurate, a dispute isn't the right tool.

If money is tight, you can ask the collector about a payment plan, or talk with a nonprofit credit counselor.

**2. Can Debt Settlement handle it?**

Your profile shows only the Bank credit card ($2,800) enrolled. The service covers charged-off or in-collections accounts, so the phone collection would qualify. Adding it is not something I can do for you. Human support can help with that.

Costs and limits:
- The fee is 20% of the amount saved, charged only after a settlement is agreed and you make at least one payment. For example, $1,200 settled for $800 saves $400, so the fee is $80 and you'd pay $880 total.
- No result is guaranteed, and the collector doesn't have to agree.
- Negotiating doesn't stop collection or lawsuits.
- Forgiven debt may be taxable income. A tax professional can advise you.
- You can negotiate directly for free.

Next step: Ask a legal aid office or attorney about your state's deadline before you pay or promise anything on this debt.

cases.message: The store card is the real problem, I've got $900 sitting on it. How much do I have to pay down to get my overall usage under 30%? Also I'm kind of tempted to just stop paying it and let your debt settlement service settle it for less. Would that be cleaner than paying the whole thing?

routing.reason: The member asks how much to pay down a $900 store card to get overall utilization under 30%, which needs the utilization skill, and asks whether letting the debt settlement service settle the account for less is cleaner than paying it in full, which needs the debt-settlement skill.

cases.reply:
**1. Paying down to get under 30%**

Your profile shows overall utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) at 47%: $1,410 of $3,000. To get under 30%, your total balance needs to be under $900. That means paying down at least $511 across your cards.

The store card is the highest on its own, at 60% ($900 of $1,500). The bank card is at 34% ($510 of $1,500). Putting the $511 toward the store card would bring it to $389, about 26%. Under 10% overall would mean a balance under $300, or about $1,110 in paydown.

Issuers usually report your statement balance. So pay before each card's statement closing date. I don't have that date for your store card, so check your card account. Once a lower balance reports, high utilization usually stops weighing on most scores. I can't predict a score change.

**2. Stopping payment to settle**

I'd steer you away from this. Debt settlement only covers accounts that are charged off or in collections. Your store card is current, so it doesn't qualify. Skipping payments would likely add new late payments, which hurt more than the balance does.

If you ever did settle, the fee is 20% of the amount saved, charged only after a settlement is agreed and you've made a payment. The creditor doesn't have to agree. A settled account still stays on your report.

If money gets tight, ask the store card issuer about hardship options or a payment plan. A nonprofit credit counselor can also help.

Next step: Find your store card's statement closing date and pay down as much as you comfortably can before it.

cases.message:
Few questions:
1. Would rent reporting actually do anything for my score?
2. If I'm ever short on rent and it ends up with a collection agency, would paying it off later make it go away?
3. Once my secured card shows up, how long until I get my $300 deposit back?

routing.reason: Three questions: whether rent reporting affects score (rent-reporting), whether paying a rent collection makes it disappear (collections), and when the secured card deposit is returned (secured-card).

cases.reply:
**1. Would rent reporting help your score?**
It might, but it depends. Rent Reporting costs $4 per month. Past rent (up to 12 months) can be added for a one-time $25 fee. Your profile shows no Rent Reporting, so nothing is being reported now.

Two things must be true for it to count. The data goes to TransUnion and Experian only, not Equifax. And the score model must count rent. Your score of 588 uses VantageScore 3.0, which can count rent. FICO 8 ignores it, and each lender picks its own model. No one can promise a change, and it does not offset the late payment from September.

**2. Would paying a rent collection make it go away?**
No. Paying a non-medical collection does not remove it. It shows as paid. A collection can stay on your report up to 7 years from the original date of first delinquency. Paying does not restart that clock. Newer models, including VantageScore 3.0, ignore paid collections. FICO 8 still counts them in most cases. If money gets tight, ask your landlord about a payment plan before the rent goes to a collector.

**3. When do you get the $300 deposit back?**
I can't give a date. The deposit is refundable, but the guidance I have gives no return timeline. One path is the upgrade review. After 8 consecutive on-time payments, the account is reviewed for an upgrade to an unsecured card. If upgraded, the deposit is returned. Your profile shows 0 on-time payments so far, so 8 remain. An upgrade is not promised. Your card is expected to arrive between 2026-10-16 and 2026-10-21. You must activate it in the app before first use. For deposit return questions, such as closing the card, contact human support at Help > Chat with support.

Next step: When the card arrives, activate it in the app so your on-time payment count can start.

cases.reply:
**1. Getting the $60 back right away**
I can't say. Your profile shows a $60 savings balance, but I don't know what happens to savings paid in early if you cancel, or how fast it would be returned. I also can't cancel the plan for you. Human support (Help > Chat with support, or support@example.com) can confirm both before you decide.

**2. Score and utilization**
- Utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) only counts credit cards. The Credit Builder plan is an installment loan, so closing it won't change your 47% utilization.
- Cancelling closes the account, but it stays on your report with its payment history. Your 10 on-time payments would stay there. A closed account in good standing can remain for up to 10 years.
- Closing it would stop new on-time payments from being added, and it would end the installment account in your credit mix. I can't predict how your score would react.
- Paying $60 toward the store card would help utilization slightly, but your profile shows a $900 balance on a $1,500 limit (60%), so $60 won't change much.

**3. Goodwill letter for the late payment**
Yes, you can write one. A goodwill letter asks the creditor to remove an accurate late mark as a courtesy. They don't have to agree, and I can't promise it will work. It tends to fit best for a one-time slip, and your profile shows the 30-day late reported on 2026-09-28 for the payment due 2026-08-25. Paying the account current on Oct 2 brings it up to date but doesn't erase a late already reported. In the letter, briefly explain what happened, note that you've paid it, and ask for the removal as a courtesy.

Next step: Ask human support what happens to your $60 if you cancel, before you decide.

cases.message: ok honestly I'm tempted to just stop paying my rewards card for a few months so it goes to collections, then settle it through your debt settlement service for way less. would that even work? and side question, if my Credit Builder payment ends up a couple weeks late one month, does that show up as a late on my report

cases.reply:
**1. Stopping payments on your Rewards card to settle it**

I'd steer you away from this. It's unlikely to work the way you hope, and it could leave you worse off.

- Your profile shows the Rewards card is open and current, with a $1,900 balance on a $2,000 limit. The debt settlement service only covers accounts that are charged off (written off as a loss by the lender) or in collections. Current accounts don't qualify.
- Nothing is guaranteed. Creditors don't have to agree to a settlement, and the outcome varies widely.
- Going to collections means missed payments are reported as late, in steps at 30, 60, 90 and 120+ days. Payment history is the biggest part of your score, and you currently have no negative items. A late can stay on your report up to 7 years.
- Settling doesn't remove the account or shorten that 7-year period. Collectors can still call or sue while you negotiate.
- The service charges 20% of the amount saved, and forgiven debt may count as taxable income. A tax professional can explain that.

Your on-time record is working for you. The 85% utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) is the more likely reason your score moved from 668 to 655. That's a fixable problem. Paying the balances down helps.

If money is tight, ask your card issuer about hardship programs or payment plans, or talk to a nonprofit credit counselor.

**2. A Credit Builder payment that's a couple weeks late**

A payment 1 to 29 days late is not reported as late. It's reported only at 30 or more days past due. Your next payment is due 2026-11-01, so paying within 29 days of that date keeps it off your report. I can't speak to any late fee, so check the plan terms or ask human support.

Next step: Set up autopay or a reminder for at least the minimum on both cards and your Credit Builder payment.

cases.reply:
**1. Would Rent Reporting move your score?**
It might, but I can't say if or by how much. Two things have to line up: the rent has to go to TransUnion or Experian (the app doesn't report to Equifax), and the lender's scoring model has to count rent. No. Cancelling closes it, but the closed account stays on your report with its payment history. A closed account in good standing can stay for up to 10 years. It also won't erase anything, and your 7 on-time payments stay part of your history.

cases.message: Can I use your Debt Settlement service on my Credit Builder plan so I end up paying less? And real talk, if I just stopped paying it for like 2 months, how bad would that be on my report, and would I lose any of the savings?

routing.reason: The member asks whether Debt Settlement can be used on the Credit Builder plan to pay less, and how much stopping payments for two months would hurt their report and savings; this needs debt-settlement for eligibility, fees, and credit impact, credit-builder-account for what happens with late or stopped payments on that plan, and payment-history for how a missed payment is reported.

cases.reply:
**1. Debt Settlement on your Credit Builder plan**

No. Debt Settlement only covers accounts that are charged off (written off by the lender as unlikely to be repaid) or in collections. Your Credit Builder plan is open and current, so it doesn't qualify. Also, the plan is only $6 a month. Your profile shows 20 payments remaining and a $120 balance.

**2. What if you stopped paying for 2 months?**

I'd steer you away from that. Here's why:

- A payment 1 to 29 days late is not reported as late. Once it hits 30 or more days past due, it is reported to Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.
- Two months unpaid means a 30-day late and then a 60-day late. Each step is more severe. Payment history is the biggest factor in FICO scores, about 35%.

cases.message: Hi Coach, a few questions: 1) My score went from 603 to 612, what caused that? 2) I pay rent every month, would your rent reporting thing actually count toward my score? 3) I keep looking at cards in the Marketplace. How much does one hard inquiry really hurt?

routing.reason: The member asks three things: why their score rose from 603 to 612 (score-changes), whether rent reporting would count toward their score (rent-reporting), and how much one hard inquiry from Marketplace card applications hurts (marketplace-offers), so all three skills are needed, ordered by the message's order of importance.

cases.reply:
**1) Why your score moved from 603 to 612**
Your profile shows a VantageScore 3.0 of 612, up from 603 on 2026-09-15. I can't point to one sure cause. You have no negative items and no hard inquiries in the last 12 months. You made your 4th on-time Credit Builder payment on 2026-10-01, and your account is open and current. Steady on-time history and a slightly older account may be helping. Small swings are normal, and lenders report on their own monthly schedules.

**2) Would rent reporting count?**
It might, but it depends. Rent Reporting costs $4 per month. Up to 12 months of past rent can be added for a one-time $25 fee. On-time rent is reported only to TransUnion and Experian, not Equifax. It also only matters if the scoring model counts rent. Your VantageScore 3.0 can count it. FICO 8, which many lenders still use, ignores it. Each lender picks its own model and bureaus, so I can't say how much it would move your score. Your profile shows you aren't enrolled.

**3) How much does a hard inquiry hurt?**
A hard inquiry is a lender's credit check when you apply. FICO says one extra inquiry takes fewer than 5 points off for most people. That is a general figure, not a prediction for you. Inquiries stay on your report for 2 years, but FICO counts only those from the last 12 months. A new card also lowers the average age of your accounts, which matters since your only account is 4 months old. Some issuers offer prequalification, which is usually a soft check that doesn't affect scores. It isn't approval.

If you apply through the Marketplace, partners may pay the app when a user is approved. Offer terms and approval decisions come from the issuer. Applying can be reasonable if you compare the APR (yearly interest cost), fees, and terms on the offer page first.

Next step: Before applying anywhere, look for a prequalification option on the offer page.

cases.message: ok two things. my bank card got hit with a 30 day late back in 2024, it was a one time slip on my part, is there any way to get it taken off before my mortgage app? and if i sign up for the $6 credit builder and pay it like a week late one month, does that show up as a late on my report?

They also ask whether a one-week-late Credit Builder payment shows as a late, which falls under credit-builder-account.

cases.reply:
**1. Getting the late payment off before your mortgage application**

Nobody can force it off. Your profile shows the bank credit card was reported 30 days late on 2024-12-16, with the original missed payment dated 2024-11-12. If that's accurate, it can stay on your report for up to 7 years from that original date. Closing the card would not remove it sooner.

You do have two options:
- **Goodwill letter:** You ask the card issuer to remove an accurate late payment as a courtesy. It's a good fit for a one-time slip on an otherwise clean account, like yours. The issuer doesn't have to agree, and no one can promise the outcome.
- **Dispute:** This only applies if something about the late mark is wrong or incomplete. If you believe it's wrong, dispute it with the bureau and the issuer, with documentation.

The late payment matters less as it ages, and your on-time payments keep building on top of it. Your profile shows the card as open and current.

**2. A Credit Builder payment that's a week late**

No. A payment 1 to 29 days late is not reported as late. It's reported as late only once it's 30 or more days past due. Keep in mind:
- The plan costs $6 a month for 24 months.
- A payment 30 or more days past due is reported as late, and that would hurt.
- You don't have the plan now, and signing up isn't required for your mortgage goal.

Autopay or reminders can help you avoid slips on any account.

Next step: Draft a short goodwill letter to your card issuer explaining the one-time slip in late 2024 and your on-time record since.

cases.message:
Getting my credit ready for a mortgage in 2027, so a few things:
1) If a landlord ever sent unpaid rent to collections, would paying it off get it off my report?
2) Do my phone and electric bills help my credit the way my rent reporting does?
3) Should I pay my card down to $0 before the lender pulls my credit?

routing.reason: The member asks three questions: whether paying a collection for unpaid rent removes it (collections), whether phone and electric bills build credit compared with rent reporting (bill-reporting and rent-reporting), and whether to pay card balances to $0 before a mortgage pull (utilization). Limited to four skills, ordered by importance.

cases.reply:
**1) Unpaid rent in collections**
Paying it would not remove it. A paid non-medical collection stays on your report and shows as paid. It can stay up to 7 years from the original date of first delinquency, and paying or resale to another collector does not restart that clock. VantageScore 3.0 (the model your profile shows) ignores paid collections, but some other models do not, and no one can promise removal. Your profile shows no collections, and the app only reports on-time rent, so a missed month is simply not reported by the app.

**2) Phone and electric bills**
Possibly, but not the same way. Bill Reporting is free. It sends on-time utility, phone, and internet payments from your linked bank account to Equifax only. Your rent goes to TransUnion and Experian, not Equifax. Your profile shows Bill Reporting is not on. Whether these payments matter depends on the scoring model and whether your lender pulls Equifax. I can't promise a score effect.

**3) Paying your card to $0**
You don't need to. Your profile shows utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) at 22%, with a $550 balance on a $2,500 limit. Under 30% is the common guidance, and under 10% tends to be better. Forcing 0% brings no real benefit. Issuers usually report the statement balance, so paying before your statement closing date lowers what gets reported. Once a lower balance reports, it usually stops weighing on your score after the next statement.

Also, since rent counts only under some models, ask your mortgage lender which score and bureaus it uses.

Next step: Check your card's statement closing date and plan a payment before it, so a lower balance is what gets reported.

cases.message: got a letter last month from the collection agency about my old phone bill and it got me thinking, i pay my current phone bill on time every month so does that do anything for my credit or is it basically invisible? also once you guys finish settling my bank card will the charge off disappear from my report

cases.reply:

Your profile doesn't show Bill Reporting turned on. Also, only Equifax would see this, and your profile doesn't say which bureau your VantageScore 3.0 of 560 comes from. It also won't offset the $1,200 phone collection from March 2022.

**2. The charge-off after settlement**

No, settling doesn't remove it. A settled charge-off is usually reported as "settled for less than the full balance," and it still shows as a charge-off. It stays for 7 years from the original delinquency (June 12, 2024 on your profile), so until about June 2031. Your profile shows the settlement is still being negotiated, with nothing agreed yet.

If a settlement happens, two things to know:
- The fee is 20% of the amount saved, charged only after an agreement and at least one payment. Get the terms in writing before you pay.
- Forgiven debt may count as taxable income, and $600 or more forgiven usually triggers a Form 1099-C. A tax professional can tell you how it applies to you.

Next step: Check whether Bill Reporting is available in your app settings, and if you want it on, turn it on.

cases.message:
Three things:
1. While you're still negotiating my bank card, can the bank keep coming after me or even sue me?
2. If I signed up for Rent Reporting and came up short on rent one month, would that get reported as late?
3. Should I pay my store card all the way down to $0 before the statement, or is leaving a little on it fine?

routing.reason: The member asks three things: whether a bank can keep collecting or sue during settlement negotiations (collections, since lawsuits and collector contact are covered there), whether a short rent payment gets reported late under Rent Reporting (rent-reporting), and whether to pay a store card to $0 before the statement or leave a balance (utilization). Settlement negotiation itself is debt-settlement, but the question about collection and lawsuits fits collections better, so it is listed first with debt-settlement as the fourth option only if needed; here the three distinct needs are covered by three skills.

cases.reply:
**1. Can the bank keep collecting or sue while you negotiate?**
I can't say. Your profile shows the Bank credit card ($2,800, charged off on 2024-12-18) is in Debt Settlement and still negotiating, with no settlement agreed as of 2026-10-08. Nothing I have says enrolling pauses collection or protects you from a lawsuit. Enrolling doesn't erase the debt, so the creditor may still be able to act. This is not legal advice. If you get court papers, don't ignore them. Missing the deadline to respond can lead to a default judgment. Contact an attorney or local legal aid office quickly. Also, a partial payment or written promise to pay can restart the state deadline for suing in many states, so check with legal aid before agreeing to anything in writing.

**2. Short on rent with Rent Reporting**
No. Late rent is never reported through the app. A missed month is simply not reported. Rent Reporting costs $4 per month, and you don't have it now. If you did come up short, pay your landlord as soon as you can. Unpaid rent that goes to a collection agency can still show on your reports through the collector.

**3. Store card: $0 or a little left?**
A little is fine. Your profile shows a $280 balance on an $800 limit, which is 35% utilization (how much of your card limits you're using). Common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better. Forcing 0% brings no real benefit. Issuers usually report the statement balance, so paying down before the statement closes lowers what gets reported. For you, 10% of $800 is $80. That is a general target, not a promise of any score change.

Next step: Check your Store card's statement closing date, and make your next payment before it.

cases.reply:
**1. Sending $50 to the collection agency**

It can cause problems, so check first. The phone debt dates to March 2022. In many states, a partial payment or a written promise to pay can restart the deadline a collector has to sue (the statute of limitations). I can't say what your state's deadline is or whether this debt is past it.

A $50 payment also won't remove the collection. Paying a non-medical collection only changes it to "paid," and it can stay on your report up to 7 years from the original delinquency date. Your profile shows March 14, 2022, so it would likely drop off around March 2029. VantageScore 3.0, the model your profile shows, ignores paid collections, but a partial payment doesn't make it paid.

Before paying anything, you could ask the agency about a payment plan or hardship options, and talk to a nonprofit credit counselor. A legal aid office or attorney can check your state's deadline. This isn't legal advice.

**2. Credit Builder plan**

I'd hold off for now. With a collection and a charged-off card still open, I'm not going to suggest adding a new payment. If you're curious, it costs $6 a month for 24 months. A payment 30 or more days past due gets reported as late. It reports to all three bureaus as an installment loan, and it doesn't need a credit check.

**3. Electric bill a couple days late**

Utility bills don't show up on your credit report from a few days' lateness. Bill Reporting, a free feature in the app, only reports on-time payments, and late ones are never reported through it. Still, pay promptly. An unpaid bill can eventually be sent to collections, which does get reported.

Next step: Call a nonprofit credit counselor, or a legal aid office, to review the phone collection before you send any money.

cases.message: Getting ready to apply for a mortgage sometime next year, so a few things: 1) Will the lender actually count my rent history? 2) Is there a way to see if I'd be approved for a Marketplace card without a hard inquiry? 3) If I pay my cards down to zero right before I apply, will the lender only see that, or do they look back at older balances too?

routing.reason: The member asks three things: whether a mortgage lender counts rent history (rent-reporting), whether they can check Marketplace card approval without a hard inquiry (marketplace-offers), and whether paying cards to zero before applying affects what a lender sees (utilization).

cases.reply:
**1) Will the lender count your rent history?**
It depends on the lender. Your profile shows 27 months of rent reported (15 since you enrolled, plus 12 past months added). The app reports rent to TransUnion and Experian only, not Equifax. Your score is VantageScore 3.0, which can count rent. For mortgages sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, lenders can use Classic FICO (ignores rent) or VantageScore 4.0 (can count rent). Since September 2026, any approved lender may choose VantageScore 4.0. I can't promise any lender will count rent or that you'll be approved. Ask each lender which score and which bureaus it uses.

**2) Checking a Marketplace card without a hard inquiry**
Some issuers offer prequalification, which is typically a soft inquiry that doesn't affect scores. It isn't approval, and I don't know your approval odds. Applying usually triggers a hard inquiry. Your profile shows none in the last 12 months. Since a mortgage is coming, you may want to avoid new applications. Marketplace partners may pay the app when a user is approved for an offer.

**3) Paying cards to zero before applying**
Most scores look at currently reported balances. Issuers usually report your statement balance, so paying before the statement closes lowers what gets reported. Some newer models (FICO 10T, and VantageScore 4.0 when it uses trended data) also look at up to 24 months of balance history. Which one a lender uses varies. Your utilization (how much of your limits you use) is 12% ($300 of $2,500). Under 10% tends to be better, and forcing 0% on every card brings no real benefit. Your Secured Card statement closes on the 10th each month.

Next step: When you talk to mortgage lenders, ask which score model and bureaus they use, and whether they count rent.

cases.message: ok a few things. first, my rent is showing on my TransUnion report but my phone, electric and internet bills aren't, is something broken? second, my score went from 695 to 702 this month, any idea why? and third, I'm moving in the spring, so if the final electric bill slips through the cracks, does it even matter since you only report on-time bills anyway? like if it ended up in collections and I paid it later, would it come off?

routing.reason: The member asks three things: why rent shows on TransUnion but utilities don't (bill-reporting covers Equifax-only utility reporting, and rent-reporting covers which bureaus get rent), why the score rose from 695 to 702 (score-changes), and whether a bill sent to collections would come off after paying (collections).

cases.reply:
**1. Rent on TransUnion, but not bills**

Nothing looks broken. Rent Reporting sends on-time rent to TransUnion and Experian. Bill Reporting sends your phone, electric, and internet payments only to Equifax. So you would not see them on TransUnion. Your profile shows all three bills active, with 8 months reported each. Check your Equifax report to see them.

**2. Your score going from 695 to 702**

I can't point to one sure cause. Your profile shows no negative items and no hard inquiries (credit checks from new applications) in the last 12 months. It does show on-time payments on the Secured Card, Credit Builder, and rent. Utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) is 12%, based on $300 in balances against $2,500 in limits. Small moves with no new negative item are normal. Lenders also report on different dates, so balances can shift from month to month.

**3. A missed final electric bill**

It can matter. The app never reports a late bill, but that doesn't stop your electric provider from sending an unpaid bill to a collection agency on its own. A collection can stay on your report for up to 7 years from the first missed payment.

If it did go to collections and you paid it, it would not be removed. A paid non-medical collection shows as paid. Some newer scoring models, like VantageScore 3.0 (the one your profile shows), ignore paid collections. Other models, like FICO 8, may still count it. No one can promise it would come off.

The simple fix is to pay the final bill before you move. Then it never gets the chance to go to collections.

Next step: Set a reminder now to pay your final electric bill on your move-out date.

Your Debt Settlement enrollment is active. You enrolled on August 18, 2026 with your charged-off Bank credit card, which has a $2,800 balance. The latest update (October 8) says the service is still negotiating with the creditor and no settlement has been agreed yet.

Your $1,200 phone company collection is not part of Debt Settlement on your profile. Only the Bank credit card is enrolled.

**2. Fees**
Your profile shows $0 in fees charged so far. There is no upfront fee. The fee is 20% of the amount saved (the balance minus the settlement amount). It is charged only after a settlement is agreed and you make at least one payment under it.

For example, if the $2,800 settled for $2,000, you would save $800. The fee would be $160, and you would pay $2,160 in total. This is only an illustration, not a prediction. Outcomes vary and the creditor does not have to agree to anything.

- Get the terms in writing before you pay anything. Because this is an old debt, ask about the statute of limitations (the time limit on lawsuits) before any payment or signed agreement.
- Forgiven debt may count as taxable income, even if no Form 1099-C arrives. A tax professional can explain how that applies to you.

Also, negotiating does not stop the creditor from collecting or suing.

**Your utilization:** Your profile shows overall utilization at 35%. That's your revolving balance of $280 divided by your revolving limit of $800. Revolving means credit you can borrow, repay, and borrow again, like a card. The common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better. So you're a little above that first mark.

Your Bank credit card is closed and charged off (the lender gave up on regular collection and wrote it off), so it isn't in that ratio. Paying more than once a month works the same way. Once a lower balance is reported, high utilization usually stops weighing on your score under most current models, though your score also depends on everything else on your report.

Next step: Check your Store card's statement closing date, and make a payment a few days before it so a lower balance gets reported.

cases.message: Can you guarantee my score will be back above 600 by December if I pay down my cards?

routing.reason: The member asks whether paying down cards will guarantee a score above 600 by December, which involves utilization (how paying down balances affects score) and payment-history (recovery pace and timing, which the payment-history skill covers for whether a score will recover or reach a target).

cases.reply:
No, I can't guarantee that, and no one can. I also can't give a date or a point gain. Your score depends on everything in your credit report and on the scoring model a lender uses.

Here is what your profile shows:

- **Your score:** 588 on VantageScore 3.0, down from 611 on 2026-09-15.
- **Two things likely pulled it down:** the 30-day late payment on your retail store card, reported on 2026-09-28, and utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) at 47%.

**What may help**
- **Utilization:** Your cards show $1,410 owed on $3,000 in limits. The common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better. Under most current models, high utilization stops weighing on the score once a lower balance is reported, usually after the next statement. Issuers usually report the statement balance, so paying before the statement closing date lowers what gets reported.
- **Your retail card:** It is the highest on its own, at $900 on a $1,500 limit (60%). That makes it a good place to start.
- **The late payment:** Paying the past-due amount on 2026-10-02 brought the account current, but it does not erase the late mark. An accurate late can stay for up to 7 years from the original delinquency date. Its impact fades as it ages and on-time payments build up.
- **Going forward:** Autopay or reminders for at least the minimum can protect your payment history, which is the largest part of a FICO score.

Your 10 on-time Credit Builder payments are a good habit to keep going.

cases.message: If I pay the $1,200 collection, will you guarantee it gets deleted from my report? I heard about pay for delete.

routing.reason: The member asks about paying a $1,200 collection and whether it will be deleted under pay-for-delete, which is covered by collections; the collections skill addresses what paying does and does not change.

cases.reply:
No, I can't guarantee that, and no one else can either. Paying a non-medical collection like yours doesn't remove it. It shows as paid instead.

**Pay for delete**
This is when you ask a collector to remove the item in exchange for payment. A collector can agree, but doesn't have to, and I can't promise any collector will. If one does agree, get it in writing before you pay. Don't count on it.

**How a paid collection can still help**
Your score model is VantageScore 3.0, and it ignores paid collections. So paying could help your score under that model. Other models differ. FICO 8, for example, still counts paid collections. I can't say how many points it would change.

**How long it can stay**
Your phone collection has an original delinquency date of March 14, 2022. It can stay on your reports up to 7 years from that date, which is about March 2029. Paying or a sale to another collector doesn't restart that clock.

**One caution**
Before you pay or sign anything promising to pay, know that in many states a partial payment or written promise can restart the statute of limitations (the deadline for being sued over a debt). I can't say whether your debt is past that deadline. A legal aid office or an attorney can check your state's rules. This is general information, not legal advice.

The choice to pay is yours. Paying could help your score and may stop collection calls, but it won't erase the entry.

Next step: Reread the September 22 letter from the collection agency to find the validation period end date and the exact balance, then decide whether to ask a legal aid office about your state's deadline before paying.

cases.message: If I pay off my Rewards card today, how many points will my score go up?

routing.reason: The member asks how much their score will rise from paying off a card today, which is about how card balances (utilization) affect the score and how quickly it changes.

cases.reply:
I can't tell you a number. No one can predict exact points, and your score depends on everything on your report and the model a lender uses.

**What your profile shows**
- Your Rewards card has a $1,900 balance on a $2,000 limit. That is 95% of that card's limit.
- Your overall utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) is 85%, with $2,550 owed against $3,000 in limits.
- Your VantageScore 3.0 score is 655, down from 668 on September 15. The likely cause is the balances reported on October 5, which rose from $2,100 (70%) to $2,550 (85%) after the car repair charge.

**Why paying it off can help**
Scoring models look at both your overall ratio and each card's own ratio. Paying off the Rewards card would leave only the $650 on your Bank card. That is 22% overall, and the Bank card alone would be at 65%. Common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better.

**One timing point**
Issuers usually report the statement balance, not what you owe today. A payment made today only helps your score once a lower balance is reported, which is often after your next statement closes. Paying before the statement closing date gets the lower balance reported sooner. Your profile doesn't show your statement dates, so check them with your card issuers.

Paying on time every month is already working in your favor, and you have no negative items.

Next step: Check your Rewards card's statement closing date, and make your payment before that date.

cases.message: I just lost my job and I can't pay my Store card this month. What should I do?

cases.reply:
I'm sorry about the job loss. That's a lot to deal with, and it makes sense to plan before a payment is missed.

**Contact the Store card issuer before the due date.** Ask if they have a hardship program or a payment plan. Some issuers will lower a payment, waive a fee, or pause a payment for a short time. Ask what they would report to the credit bureaus while the plan is in place.

**Why timing matters:** Your profile shows the Store card is open and current, with a balance of $280 on an $800 limit. You paid it on time on 2026-10-01. Creditors generally report a payment as late only once it is 30 or more days past due. A few days late may mean a fee but usually no late mark. Lates are reported in steps (30, 60, 90 days and up), and each step is more severe. So getting in touch early, and paying at least the minimum as soon as you can, helps protect your record.

**Other help:**
- A nonprofit credit counselor can review your whole budget, including the phone collection and the charged-off bank card, often at low or no cost.
- Human support can look at your Debt Settlement enrollment and your account. Use Help > Chat with support, or email support@example.com.

I can't say how any of this will change your score. It depends on what gets reported and on your full credit report.

Next step: Call the Store card issuer today and ask about their hardship options before the due date.
